title: Energy-Based Models for Predicting Mutational Effects on Proteins

problem.claim: Predicting changes in protein binding free energy is important for protein engineering, protein-protein interaction engineering, and drug discovery.

gap.claim: Computing the complete conformational distribution of a protein complex is generally regarded as intractable.

contributions.claim: The approach predicts ΔΔG by decomposing it into a sequence-based component estimated by an inverse folding model and a structure-based component estimated by an energy model.
The decomposition uses an equilibrium assumption between bound and unbound states to simplify estimation of state degeneracies.
The method connects sequence log-odds-ratio-based ΔΔG prediction with a statistical-mechanics-grounded ΔΔE term through an energy-based physical inductive bias.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report superiority over existing state-of-the-art structure- and sequence-based deep learning methods for ΔΔG prediction.
The authors report superiority in antibody optimization against SARS-CoV-2.

narrative_sequence.summary: ΔΔG prediction is presented as important for protein and PPI engineering.
Prior approaches relate ΔΔG to entropy using probabilities of biologically important objects.
Full conformational-distribution estimation is described as generally intractable.
The proposed approach uses energy-based models, a sequence/structure decomposition, and an equilibrium assumption.
The authors report improved ΔΔG prediction and SARS-CoV-2 antibody optimization relative to existing deep learning methods.

source_observation.claim: The method combines a sequence-based inverse folding component with a structure-based energy component.

interpretation.claim: Combining complementary representations may make a difficult physical prediction task more tractable.

application.claim: For related molecular prediction problems, consider decomposing the target into sequence- and structure-dependent terms when each can be modeled separately.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when the equilibrium assumption is valid or whether the decomposition generalizes beyond the reported setting.

unknowns: Datasets, evaluation metrics, and quantitative results are not specified.
The compared state-of-the-art methods and experimental settings are not specified.
The validity and limitations of the bound/unbound equilibrium assumption are not described.
